title: Circular Cities: Fix It, Don't Trash It
summary:
Suppose your shoe splits, or a favorite toy breaks. Do you throw it away — or fix it? Now imagine a whole city asking that question about almost everything.

That is the idea behind circular cities. About 100 communities around the world try to keep materials in use as long as possible, through repairs, reuse, and recycling, instead of sending them to the trash.

Most products follow a straight line. Companies gather raw materials, factories build products, people use them until they break, and then they are thrown away. Only a very small share get recycled. Circular cities aim for a closed loop instead.

Landfills are part of the problem. They are filling up, and most give off methane, a gas that warms the planet. Replacement products create still more pollution.

Austin, Texas, shows what a city can do. It runs a yearly toy-repair clinic and fix-it workshops. Amsterdam hopes to have almost no waste by 2050. As big buyers, cities can ask companies for greener goods. Just because something is broken does not mean its use has to stop.
why_it_matters: When your toy or shoe breaks, fixing it instead of throwing it away can help keep your city cleaner.
